transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-03 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Marta (Product), Samir (NovaFin), Lena (NovaFin), Marcus (NovaFin), Anya (NovaFin)

00:00 Jordan Blake: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll run through a targeted workshop today on large context and high throughput. we're expecting a mix of product + infra questions so feel free to jump in.
00:28 Samir Patel: thanks, Jordan. quick context — NovaFin is prototyping a risk summarization pipeline that needs to ingest whole financial books, sometimes 70–120k tokens, and run multi-pass reasoning plus a few parallel rerankers. so the trio of latency, cost, and reliability are all big concerns.
00:50 Priya Nair: ok got it. the key pieces we'll demo are: how Redwood's runtime handles extended KV cache for long contexts, behavior under sustained TPS, what triggers backpressure in streaming, and how timeouts are surfaced. we'll also show Console Optimize tips.
01:12 Marcus Young: real quick, what counts as long context? we've seen docs call it many things. is 100k realistic?
01:22 Priya Nair: yes, 100k is in scope. we treat context as a sequence length and if the model supports it we stream tokens but maintain a KV cache. caveat: large contexts increase memory per request and affect batching efficiency.
01:42 Lena Cho: and for autoscaling, do you spin up more GPUs for big requests or throttle? we've got constraints in our VPC.
01:52 Ethan Cole: short answer: mixture. runtime prefers to route by capacity tier. for Dedicated pilot you can reserve pools, and routing rules avoid sending giant contexts to small nodes. if capacity is saturated, fallback routing to a compatible smaller-context variant or queued backpressure happens.
02:12 Anya Volk: on compliance, we need audit logs for the request payloads that touch PII — does that increase latency?
02:21 Marta Ruiz: audit logs are async and pushed to your KMS-backed audit store; negligible impact on token path, but there's a small enqueue cost. we'll note it in the runbook.
02:34 Jordan Blake: quick demo plan: 1) API call with 110k token doc (simulated), 2) high TPS replay hitting the same model to show batching/backpressure, 3) streaming session and induced slow consumer to show backpressure and timeout behavior, 4) Console Optimize suggestions.
03:00 -- screen share: Redwood Console -- model selection panel --
03:24 Priya Nair: starting first test: single request, model rdx-longform-alpha, sequence len ~112k, single-shot summary. sending now.
03:40 Speaker 1: (system) request accepted, tokenizer split into 8 chunks for k/v management, kv checkpoints saved.
04:00 Priya Nair: you might see some pre-warm as kernels compile — this is normal on cold path.
04:20 Marcus Young: time to first byte?
04:26 Priya Nair: ttfb is around 800–1,200ms on our Dedicated nodes for this size (cold). warm cached execution is 200–400ms, then streaming token rate. note these are ballpark; we'll run concrete benchmarks with your corpus.
04:48 Samir Patel: curious about cost: if we keep KV cache across requests versus resending full doc, what's the delta?
04:56 Priya Nair: huge — prefix/KV caching can drop per-request compute by 3–8x depending on reuse. Console Optimize will flag high-reuse patterns and recommend pinning contexts to the same session or using our chunked retrieval feature.
05:18 -- running high TPS script now --
05:28 Ethan Cole: now we simulate sustained 220 QPS with mixed short and long requests to the same model. watch the per-node queue depth and batching util.
05:44 Lena Cho: that QPS seems high for 1 node — do you autoscale?
05:50 Ethan Cole: autoscale policy kicks in around sustained CPU/GPU util and queue latency; you can define strict SLOs to prefer latency over cost, which triggers more nodes earlier.
06:08 Speaker 2: WARNING: queue_backpressure_detected on node-3, avg queue latency 850ms.
06:18 Priya Nair: that's the runtime signaling backpressure. by default we apply progressive throttling: we reduce batch window for short requests, route large-context ones to reserved pool, and start spilling excess capacity to a fallback model.
06:35 Samir Patel: fallback model = smaller model with trimmed context? how do you keep fidelity?
06:42 Marta Ruiz: we can automatically create a trimmed variant that preserves most of reasoning by sending X most relevant chunks (our reranker picks). Optimize suggests a rerank threshold so fidelity loss is minimized; there's also A/B rollout support to evaluate quality drop.
07:01 Jordan Blake: now we intentionally slow the streaming client to show backpressure effects on server side — we'll set a 5s per-chunk consumer delay.
07:16 -- induced slow consumer --
07:30 Speaker 3: stream partially sent, client window shrinking, server holding token buffer.
07:44 Marcus Young: will that cause the server to buffer unbounded?
07:50 Priya Nair: no we have a sliding send window and maximum buffer size. once buffer exceeds threshold we start metrics and apply one of three policies: pause generation (apply backpressure to token production), drop-to-trickle (send coarse summaries), or cut to synchronous non-streaming result. selection depends on your configured fallback policy.
08:18 Anya Volk: where do we configure those policies? in Console?
08:24 Priya Nair: yes Console -> Runtime Policies -> Streaming. you can make per-route policies and there's a default global.
08:31 Samir Patel: timeouts — we've hit transient network flaps before; what's safe to set for our pipelines?
08:36 Ethan Cole: for large-context streaming, we recommend client timeout > model generation expected time + 2x variance. Example: if you expect 30s generate, set 90s for upper bound. also enable automatic retry with idempotency keys; Redwood will resume from last known KV checkpoint if the model variant supports resumes.
09:02 Lena Cho: resume from KV - is that guaranteed? wondering about partial state and non-determinism.
09:10 Priya Nair: resume is best-effort and works when the model call is deterministic and KV serialized; for non-deterministic decoders we provide a recover-mode where we regenerate last N tokens to reconcile. we'll include that nuance in the runbook.
09:36 -- Console Optimize panel --
09:42 Marta Ruiz: Optimize just flagged two suggestions: 1) switch from 32k quant-profile to 16k for mixed workloads to get better batching; 2) enable prefix caching for the top 10% of callers. those are heuristic recommendations based on your QPS shape.
10:00 Samir Patel: why would lower quant-profile improve batching? doesn't quant hurt accuracy?
10:06 Marta Ruiz: it's about kernel scheduling: some quant levels allow denser packing in memory which reduces memcpy times for medium-length sequences, improving throughput for mixed sizes. Optimize gives predicted perf deltas.
10:22 Marcus Young: let's talk SLAs — we need p99 tail latency < 2s for short queries and < 15s for long-summary flows. feasible?
10:32 Jordan Blake: feasible with Dedicated reserved capacity and tuned batching; you'll need to trade off cost. we'll model that in the pilot.
10:44 Samir Patel: competitors sometimes recommend sharding the context in-app and logic to recombine. pros/cons?
10:52 Priya Nair: app-side sharding can work but pushes complexity into your stack; Redwood's chunking and reranking are optimized for retrieval and reorder, plus we keep KV locality. Recommendation: try Redwood chunking first, fall back to app sharding if you have domain-specific heuristics.
11:10 -- customer asks for a live stress run with their QPS curve --
11:20 Jordan Blake: let's set that up in pilot. please send the QPS curve and corpus. we'll run a Dedicated pilot with reserved pool and a stress script that mimics your traffic.
11:36 Lena Cho: okay, we'll send. one more question on encryption — can KMS keys be customer-managed?
11:42 Marta Ruiz: yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for encryption at rest and for envelope encryption of audit logs.
11:50 -- later in the call we discuss observability --
12:05 Ethan Cole: Console provides per-token cost breakdown, per-route p50/p90/p99 latency, tracing hooks to link model calls to app traces, and anomaly detection tied to prompt sets. you'll be able to see when backpressure events start and which route caused it.
12:34 Samir Patel: curious on error modes — what are the common causes of timeouts?
12:40 Priya Nair: common causes are: consumer slowness (backpressure), sudden change in sequence length distribution causing queueing, microcode/kernel cache thrash on very heterogeneous workloads, and network egress spikes. mitigation: reserve pools, limit per-session max tokens, apply adaptive batching, and pre-warm kernels.
13:05 Marcus Young: any hard limits on token length?
13:10 Priya Nair: depends on model; our rdx-longform supports up to 200k in some configs but you should expect higher mem and lower batch capacity. we usually test at your corpus size.
13:26 Anya Volk: in the security review we need an SOC2 addendum and encryption attestation — can you share that?
13:34 Jordan Blake: yes we'll attach our security pack; Jordan to share security docs and SOC2 addendum in the follow-up.
13:46 -- recap and next steps --
13:50 Jordan Blake: recap: 1) Redwood can handle 100k+ contexts with KV caching and chunking; 2) backpressure is signaled and mitigated via routing, throttles, and fallback models; 3) Console/Optimize can recommend quant/profile and caching rules; 4) we'll run a Dedicated pilot with NovaFin corpus and stress curve.
14:18 Samir Patel: great thank you.
14:25 Jordan Blake: thanks everyone; we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and pilot proposal.
14:30 -- call ends --

Notes: Transcription contains occasional mis-heards: "K V cash" for KV cache, "quant-profile" sometimes heard as "quantify profile", and speaker labels were auto-assigned (Speaker 1/2/3). Shared artifacts referenced during call: https://redwood.app/decks/novafin-long-context-workshop (deck), https://redwood.app/benchmarks/novafin-longcontext-2026-06 (benchmark spreadsheet).

End of transcript.
